Lessons.Title: Factor Pairs
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade 4 U01 Lesson 2, IM K–5 Math First Edition 2021: the target is to find all whole-number factor pairs by drawing every distinct rectangular array of a FIXED area. The learner-facing source Student Task Statements PDF is three pages. This Edulytics guidance is independently authored, not a copy of publisher artwork.

Warm-up — Number Talk (10 min): mentally find 2×7, 4×7, 3×7, 7×7. Explain strategies. For example 3×7 + 4×7 = 7×7. Teacher shows one expression at a time, elicits multiple strategies, and records them.

Activity 1 — How Many Rectangles? (20 min): divide students into eight groups A–H and assign TWO areas per group: A 11 and 27; B 25 and 5; C 16 and 8; D 9 and 18; E 24 and 12; F 14 and 28; G 15 and 30; H 19 and 20 (all square units). Use tiles and centimeter grid paper; independently/with peers draw EVERY possible rectangular model for EACH area, mark sides in units and area in square units, cut and display on a separate poster for each assigned area. Do not count rotations separately.

Activity 2 — How Many Rectangles: Gallery Walk (15 min): groups walk in pairs to examine all area posters and explain mathematical comparisons using the source 'I notice…' sentence frames. For any fixed area, explicitly show why no additional positive-whole-number side pair exists. Area 21 has unordered factor pairs (1,21) and (3,7), not (7,3) as an extra rectangle. Teacher assesses completeness and quality of explanation.

Lesson synthesis (10 min): a factor pair is any pair of whole numbers whose product is the area. List all distinct pairs for 24: (1,24), (2,12), (3,8), (4,6); for 45: (1,45), (3,15), (5,9). Check candidates from 1 up to the square root to make sure no pairs are omitted. Math Community reflection (2–3 min) follows the separate Cool-down.

Edulytics ORIGINAL Cool-down (5 min, user-approved first-party substitute, not source-identical): 'A rectangle has area 18 square units. Find every unordered whole-number pair of sides and explain how you know your list is complete.' Teacher checks the three pairs and a complete explanation. A separately generated count-of-factor-pairs question is automatically gradeable; the physical drawing and explanatory reasoning are teacher-reviewed. Original publisher Cool-down is educator-gated and is not represented as verified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number factor pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pairs of positive whole numbers whose product is the given area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Each whole-number factor pair (a,b) satisfies a×b=n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rotations are not new pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Changing which side is horizontal does not create a different unordered factor pair.
KeyConcepts.Rule: List each pair only once; (3,7) and (7,3) are one pair.
KeyConcepts.Example: Area 21 has two distinct unordered pairs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proving all pairs are found
KeyConcepts.Definition: Check candidate divisors from 1 through the square root of the area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For every divisor d ≤ √n, include exactly one pair (d,n÷d); no other pair exists.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square areas
KeyConcepts.Definition: A square area may have an equal-sided pair.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If n is a perfect square, count √n × √n once.

WorkedExamples.Title: Number Talk: multiplying by seven
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 2×7,4×7,3×7 and 7×7 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use distributive reasoning and previously computed facts.

WorkedExamples.Title: All rectangles for area 21
WorkedExamples.Question: Which unique whole-number rectangles have area 21 square units?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check possible divisors in ascending order, ignoring rotations.
Steps: Stop because 4×4<21 and further widths only reverse known pairs.

WorkedExamples.Title: All pairs for 24
WorkedExamples.Question: How can your group prove it has every possible rectangular model for area 24?
Steps: 5×5=25 exceeds 24, so no unexplored pair with smaller width exists.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four unordered pairs, each with product 24.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area 25 shows the square case
WorkedExamples.Question: How many distinct rectangular factor pairs does area 25 have?
WorkedExamples.Method: Try divisors 1..5 and count each unordered pair once.
WorkedExamples.Check: 25 has factors 1,5,25 and no extra orientations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting the same rectangular model twice after rotation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source explicitly treats widths 4×6 and 6×4 as the same factor pair.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Order each pair with smaller factor first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Leaving out 1×n or omitting a square pair.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One is a factor of every positive integer, and a perfect square has a valid repeated factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Start at width 1, then test each candidate up to the square root.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Only multiplying mentally and skipping posters/gallery explanations.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original learning task requires showing all distinct rectangles, labels and a class gallery comparison.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Complete both assigned area posters and give evidence that all factor pairs were found; teacher reviews the models.

SummaryPoints: The original 2021 three-page student task was read from the PDF linked inside the local teacher source; warm-up mental products, two assigned-area drawings and gallery questions are all distinct tasks.
Eight groups A–H each take two original area targets; students draw ALL unique whole-number factor-pair rectangles per target and display separate labeled posters.
Every pair multiplies to the area; rotations are counted only once. Check divisors systematically up to the square root to prove completeness.
Teacher/partner gallery discussion and poster artwork are teacher-reviewed, not counted as automatically graded practice.
The five-minute exit ticket is independently authored by Edulytics using the same factor-pair skill, not the source-identical educator-gated publisher Cool-down.
